content: 1. Pleural effusions should be drained unless they are very small. If effusions are present on both sides of the chest, both sides should be drained. Repeated drainage may be necessary two or three times if fluid reaccumulates. Refer to specific guidelines for chest drainage. 2. The subsequent management of pleural effusions depends on the characteristics of the fluid obtained. When possible, pleural fluid should be analyzed for protein and glucose content, cell count, and differential count. It should also be examined using Gram and Ziehl-Neelsen staining, as well as bacterial and Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures. 3. In cases of lung abscess, which is a localized, thick-walled cavity in the lung containing purulent material due to necrosis and suppuration of lung parenchyma, the condition often develops in unresolved areas of pneumonia. Causes may include pulmonary aspiration, impaired clearance mechanisms, embolic phenomena, or hematogenous spread. 4. Common signs and symptoms of lung abscess include fever, pleuritic chest pain, sputum production or hemoptysis, and weight loss. On examination, findings may include reduced chest movement, decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, crackles, and bronchial breathing. Chest X-rays typically reveal a solitary, thick-walled cavity with or without an air-fluid level. Ultrasound and CT scans can help localize the lesion and guide drainage or needle aspiration. 5. Treatment of lung abscess is usually empirical and based on the patient’s underlying condition and the presumed causative organism. Antibiotics are administered, and drainage is typically performed via percutaneous tube drainage or ultrasound-guided needle aspiration. 6. Pneumothorax, characterized by air accumulation in the pleural space due to alveolar rupture or infection with gas-producing microorganisms, presents with variable symptoms depending on the extent of lung collapse, intrapleural pressure, and rapidity of onset. Examination findings may include chest bulging on the affected side, cardiac impulse shift away from the pneumothorax, decreased breath sounds, grunting, severe respiratory distress, and cyanosis in advanced cases. 7. Diagnosis of pneumothorax is confirmed with a chest X-ray. Urgent decompression with needle thoracocentesis should be performed before inserting an intercostal chest drain. Continuous positive airway pressure may be beneficial in cases of respiratory failure. 8. Coughs and colds are common, self-limiting viral infections requiring only supportive care. Antibiotics should not be given. Wheezing or stridor may occur in some children, especially infants. Most episodes resolve within 14 days. Persistent cough lasting 14 days or more may indicate tuberculosis, asthma, pertussis, or symptomatic HIV infection. 9. Wheezing, a high-pitched whistling sound on expiration caused by spasmodic narrowing of distal airways, is common in children under two years of age due to acute viral respiratory infections like bronchiolitis. In older children, wheezing is often associated with asthma. Children with wheezing but no fever, chest indrawing, or danger signs are unlikely to have pneumonia and should not receive antibiotics. 10. Bronchiolitis, a lower respiratory viral infection most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus, is characterized by airway obstruction and wheezing. It is most severe in young infants and may lead to secondary bacterial infection. Management includes oxygen therapy, supportive care, and monitoring for respiratory distress. 11. Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition with reversible airway obstruction, characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, cough, and difficulty breathing. Diagnosis is based on history and response to bronchodilators. Treatment includes rapid-acting bronchodilators and anti-inflammatory drugs. Antibiotics are only indicated if there are signs of pneumonia. 12. In severe asthma or life-threatening cases, continuous back-to-back nebulizations with salbutamol should be administered while setting up intravenous access. Oxygen therapy should maintain oxygen saturation above 95%. If salbutamol is unavailable, subcutaneous adrenaline may be used. 13. Children with respiratory distress should be reassessed after 15 minutes of treatment with a rapid-acting bronchodilator. If respiratory distress resolves, home care with inhaled salbutamol via a metered-dose inhaler and spacer device can be advised. Persistent distress warrants hospital admission for further treatment. 14. For hospitalized children with asthma, oxygen therapy, rapid-acting bronchodilators, and steroids should be promptly administered. Nebulized salbutamol or salbutamol via a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer device is recommended. In severe cases, continuous nebulization may be required. 15. Spacer devices for inhaled bronchodilators are commercially available or can be improvised using plastic bottles. Two puffs of salbutamol (200 µg) should be introduced into the spacer chamber, and the child’s mouth placed over the opening for effective delivery.
